Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

which pronoun and adjective

which one? (a question)

also which one, which of them, which of you, which of the two

classical

Phaedr. 3.7.5: aut quō cibō fēcistī tantum corporis?

quī, quae, quod

interrogative adjective · Declension on Wiktionary

which? what? (with a noun)

With a noun: quod pōculum?, which cup? Without a noun the pronoun is quis, quid, and “which of them?” is quis eōrum? or quis ex eīs?.

Other words

  • uter, utra, utrum — which (of two)?

    interrogative pronoun and adjective; genitive utrīus, dative utrī · also used · classical · Plaut. Men. 1119: Uter erātis, tūn' an ille, major?; Plaut. Aul. 321: sed uter vestrōrum est celerior? · Declension on Wiktionary

    Latin has a word for the choice between two; quis is for more than two (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • unde sīc, quaesō, nitēs? aut quō cibō fēcistī tantum corporis?

    where do you get that shine, tell me? What food has made you so big?Phaedr. 3.7.4–5

  • quem ex eīs vultis in cēnam statim fierī?

    which of them do you want made into dinner straight away?Petr. 47.2

  • Uter erātis, tūn' an ille, major?

    Which of you was the elder, you or he?Plaut. Men. 1119

  • sed uter vestrōrum est celerior? memorā mihi.

    but which of you two is quicker? Tell me.Plaut. Aul. 321

See also which, what, this one or that one?, whichever.
